h1: Link building cost in India: the ₹500 link versus the ₹25,000 link
metaTitle: Link Building Cost in India: What a Backlink Costs
metaDescription: Link building costs ₹500 to ₹25,000 a link in India. Here is what each tier really is, why one earned link costs ₹18,000, and why we never price per link.
answer: Backlinks in India are sold from ₹500 to ₹25,000 each. Below roughly ₹5,000 you're buying a placement on a site built to sell placements. One genuinely earned link costs about ₹18,000 once you count the asset, the prospecting and the thirty pitches that produced it — which is why a ₹75,000 retainer funds one or two a month, not twenty.
takeaways: Cost per link is set by **outreach hours**, not by the publisher. That's why the maths never supports twenty links a month at ₹25,000.
Google's link spam policy explicitly covers buying and selling links that pass ranking signals. Price doesn't change that — a ₹12,000 paid link is still a paid link.
One earned link costs roughly **₹18,000** fully loaded. Run that against any per-link package and the arithmetic exposes the source.
Per-link pricing pays an agency to say yes to placements it should decline. We bill link work by hours inside the retainer, never per placement.

sections.h2: Five price tiers, and what you're actually buying at each
body: Every link on sale in India falls into one of five bands. The band tells you far more than the domain rating in the seller's spreadsheet does, because DR is trivially inflated and the business model behind the site is not.

callout.title: "We have a network of publishers"
callout.body: This sentence appears in almost every cheap link proposal. It means the same fifty sites are selling to everyone in your industry, including your competitors. A footprint that obvious is exactly what spam detection is built to find.

callout.title: The test that ends the argument
callout.body: Take any link package price, divide by the number of links promised. If the answer is under ₹8,000, no outreach happened. There isn't enough money in the quote to pay for the hours, so the links came from somewhere that doesn't require hours.

sections.h2: How many links a ₹75,000 retainer honestly funds
body: Link and digital PR work typically takes 20–30% of an SEO retainer, with the rest going to technical, content and reporting. On ₹75,000 a month that's ₹15,000–₹22,500 of link budget.

At ₹18,000 fully loaded, that buys **one earned link a month, occasionally two** when a single campaign asset lands more than one placement. That is the real number, and it's the number nobody puts on a proposal because it looks small next to "25 high-DA backlinks monthly".

It looks small until you compare what each side is. Twelve earned editorial links in a year, from sites your buyers actually read, will outrank a hundred and fifty marketplace placements — and won't need cleaning up later. The full breakdown of where retainer money goes is in [what SEO services cost, one service at a time](/cost/seo-services-cost).
bullets: **₹25,000/mo link package, 20 links** → ₹1,250 per link. Tier one. You're buying a network.
**₹50,000/mo, 8 links** → ₹6,250 per link. Paid placements on real sites, most likely undisclosed.
**₹75,000/mo retainer, 1–2 links** → ₹15,000–₹22,500 per link. Outreach that actually happened.
**₹1,50,000/mo digital PR** → 3–6 placements. A campaign, not a pitch list.

sections.h2: The risk you inherit when you buy links
body: [Google's spam policies name link spam directly](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies): buying or selling links that pass ranking signals, exchanging goods or services for links, and large-scale automated link creation. Disclosure with `rel="sponsored"` or `rel="nofollow"` keeps you compliant, and simultaneously removes the ranking benefit you paid for. That trade-off is the whole story of paid links.

The practical risk in 2026 is rarely a dramatic manual penalty. It's quieter: the links get algorithmically discounted, your rankings don't move, and you spend nine months believing SEO doesn't work for your category. You paid for a signal that was neutralised on arrival.

The second risk is the cleanup. When a site does pick up a manual action for unnatural links, disavowing and removing them is slow, unglamorous work — and it's charged at the same hourly rate the outreach would have been.

callout.title: Ask where the links come from
callout.body: Not "what DA". Ask for five live examples from other clients, then open them. If the site publishes eight sponsored posts a week across unrelated industries, you have your answer in about ninety seconds.

sections.h2: Why we refuse to sell links by the unit
body: Per-link pricing sounds fair and behaves badly. It pays the agency for placements, so the agency optimises for placements — which means the cheapest source that technically counts, every time.

It also makes "no" expensive. If a publisher is wrong for your brand, or the site smells like a network, declining costs the per-link agency real money. Nobody makes that call twenty times a month when it's coming out of their margin.

And it converts a judgement into a quota. The best link opportunity in a given month might be one partnership that takes three weeks and produces a single placement. Under a per-link contract, that month looks like failure.
numbered: We bill link work as **hours inside the retainer**, at the same rate as everything else.
We report **referring domains gained and lost**, with the live URL. You can click every one.
We don't buy placements, and we don't accept a brief that requires a fixed monthly link count.

The number we're actually measured on is your **qualified leads from organic**, frozen as a trailing-90-day baseline on day one. Miss it in 90 days and we keep working free until we beat it. No promised position, ever.

callout.title: Where this sits in the price
callout.body: SEO from ₹75,000/month, smaller sites from ₹40,000, ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter. Link work is a line inside that, not an add-on. Scope detail on [our link building services](/services/link-building-services).

faqs.q: How much does a backlink cost in India?
faqs.a: Anywhere from ₹300 to ₹25,000. The band matters more than the number: under ₹800 is a network or a directory, ₹1,500–₹4,000 is a site that exists to sell posts, ₹5,000–₹12,000 is a paid placement on a real site, and ₹12,000–₹25,000 is roughly the loaded cost of earning one.

faqs.q: Is buying backlinks against Google's rules?
faqs.a: Yes. Google's spam policies specifically cover buying or selling links that pass ranking signals, including exchanging free products or services for links. Marking the link `rel="sponsored"` keeps you compliant and removes its ranking value, which is precisely why paid-link sellers don't mark them.

faqs.q: How many backlinks should I get per month?
faqs.a: Fewer than you're being sold. A ₹75,000 retainer honestly funds one to two earned links a month. Steady acquisition from relevant sites beats volume; a sudden jump from two referring domains a month to forty is a pattern, and patterns are what detection looks for.

faqs.q: Are guest posts worth paying for?
faqs.a: A guest post on a site with a real audience that would have published you anyway is worth the writing time. A guest post on a site whose business model is selling guest posts is worth nothing, regardless of its domain rating. The test is whether the site would say no to somebody.

faqs.q: What's a fair price for link building services in India?
faqs.a: ₹15,000–₹25,000 a month buys roughly one earned link. ₹40,000–₹80,000 supports a small ongoing outreach programme with an asset behind it. Above ₹1,00,000 you're funding digital PR campaigns, which produce fewer but far stronger placements plus brand search lift.

faqs.q: Do cheap backlinks actually hurt my site?
faqs.a: Usually they just do nothing, which costs you the fee plus the months you spent waiting. Real damage — a manual action for unnatural links — happens at scale or with obvious footprints. The recovery work is slower and more expensive than the links ever were.
